raw_text:
Allow usage of . (dot) character in package or library names.

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve**
Currently, Cargo will not allow `.` to be used in package or library name:
```toml
[package]
# ... other fields are omitted
name = "package.rs"
```
Will cause an error:
```
invalid character `.` in package name: `package.rs`, characters must be Unicode XID characters (numbers, `-`, `_`, or most letters)
```

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Ideal solution will be to allow `.` in package or library names, which will pretty much require a simple change in [cargo::util::restricted_names](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/blob/master/src/cargo/util/restricted_names.rs):
```rust
    for ch in chars {
        if !(unicode_xid::UnicodeXID::is_xid_continue(ch) || ch == '-') {  // || ch == '.' here
            bail!(
                "invalid character `{}` in {}: `{}`, \
                characters must be Unicode XID characters \
                (numbers, `-`, `_`, or most letters){}",  // `.` here
                ch,
                what,
                name,
                help
            );
        }
    }
```
And changed:
```rust
    for ch in chars {
        if !(unicode_xid::UnicodeXID::is_xid_continue(ch) || ch == '-' || ch == '.') {
            bail!(
                "invalid character `{}` in {}: `{}`, \
                characters must be Unicode XID characters \
                (numbers, `-`, `_`, `.` or most letters){}",
                ch,
                what,
                name,
                help
            );
        }
    }
```

**Notes**
I personally don't see any bad effects this small change might cause. `.` is a pretty much accepted character in many package managers and indexes, for example pip and PyPI in python.

raw_text:
Inconsistent reporting of [E0733] between `cargo check` and `cargo run`

### Problem

I encountered a weird issue where `cargo check` reports success, whereas `cargo run` (or build, test, etc.) results in compilation error (of course with exactly the same feature flags and `cfg(test)`).

I expected them to be consistent, (`check` should report all `build` failures as far as I undestand)

### Steps

1. Use the following minimal reproducible example
```rust
pub trait Foo {
    type Dependency: Foo;

    async fn foo() {
        Self::Dependency::foo().await;
    }
}

impl Foo for () {
    type Dependency = ();
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    <()>::foo().await;
}
```
2. Run `cargo check` - only warning is shown:
```
warning: `test-play` (bin "test-play") generated 1 warning
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.08s
```
3. `cargo build` results in error:
```
error[E0733]: recursion in an async fn requires boxing
 --> src/main.rs:4:5
  |
4 |     async fn foo() {
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
5 |         Self::Dependency::foo().await;
  |         ----------------------------- recursive call here
  |
  = note: a recursive `async fn` call must introduce indirection such as `Box::pin` to avoid an infinitely sized future

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0733`.
error: could not compile `test-play` (bin "test-play") due to 1 previous error
```

### Possible Solution(s)

Usage of associated type is an important part of repro. So the reason is somehow related to this

### Notes

_No response_

### Version

```text
cargo 1.78.0 (54d8815d0 2024-03-26)
release: 1.78.0
commit-hash: 54d8815d04fa3816edc207bbc4dd36bf18014dbc
commit-date: 2024-03-26
host: aarch64-apple-darwin
libgit2: 1.7.2 (sys:0.18.2 vendored)
libcurl: 8.1.2 (sys:0.4.72+curl-8.6.0 system ssl:(SecureTransport) LibreSSL/3.3.6)
ssl: OpenSSL 1.1.1w  11 Sep 2023
os: Mac OS 14.1.0 [64-bit]
```

Cargo-installing a binary within a workspace shows warnings about profile overrides

Situation:

- A workspace is composed of two packages: `a` and `b`.
- `b` depends on the crate `smallvec`.
- The workspace has a section mentioning `[profile.dev.package] smallvec = { opt-level = 3 }`.

When running `cargo install --path ./a`, I'm getting a warning:

```
warning: profile package spec `smallvec` in profile `dev` did not match any packages
```

This warning is printed as the package `a` doesn't depend on `smallvec`.
Running `cargo install --path ./b` works fine.

I believe that this is an issue with Cargo, as I don't think that there's a clean way to silence this warning.

Cargo config option to default to locked/frozen

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve**
I would like to be able to specify in a workspace's cargo config that by default running commands such as `cargo build` imply the `--locked`/`--frozen` option so that users/build machines don't accidentally update Cargo.lock or rely on the network.  To go along with this, cargo would need to support `--unlocked`/`--unfrozen` switches or `cargo vendor` would need to ignore `--locked`/`--frozen`.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Somewhere in `.cargo/config` I am able to specify default switches for cargo invocations and cargo has command line options to unset binary switches that may be defaulted on.

**Notes**
The intent here is to ensure that dependencies are only explicitly and deliberately updated, instead of accidentally happening if someone happens to invoke cargo incorrectly (or a tool like `rust-analyzer` does).

raw_text:
Regression in 1.94 with git dependencies having submodules

### Problem

I have a setup where my project depends on a crate as a git dependency, and this git dependency has a git submodule.

Main project contains the following in its Cargo.toml:
```toml
[dependencies.test-crate]
git = "https://github.com/okkero/test-crate.git"
rev = "382e3a6ed36417db30081c90858170d781d8574c"
```

The test-crate repo has the following `.gitmodules` file:
```
[submodule "test-submodule"]
	path = test-submodule
	url = git@github.com:okkero/test-submodule.git
```

This used to work fine before. However, in 1.94 i get this error:
```
Updating git repository `[https://github.com/okkero/test-crate.git`](https://github.com/okkero/test-crate.git%60)
error: failed to get `test-crate` as a dependency of package `cargo-test v0.1.0 (/home/runner/work/cargo-test/cargo-test)`

Caused by:
  failed to load source for dependency `test-crate`

Caused by:
  Unable to update https://github.com/okkero/test-crate.git?rev=382e3a6ed36417db30081c90858170d781d8574c

Caused by:
  failed to update submodule `test-submodule`

Caused by:
  invalid url `git@github.com:okkero/test-submodule.git`: relative URL without a base; try using `ssh://git@github.com/okkero/test-submodule.git` instead
```

Keep in mind `git@github.com:okkero/test-submodule.git` is a completely valid URL for git submodules, and works fine when using the git CLI. This only fails through cargo.

See workflow runs [here](https://github.com/okkero/cargo-test/actions/runs/23140532476/job/67215351477) (1.93) and [here](https://github.com/okkero/cargo-test/actions/runs/23140549845/job/67215413087) (1.94) demonstrating the issue.

All involved demo repos are public:
- https://github.com/okkero/cargo-test
- https://github.com/okkero/test-crate
- https://github.com/okkero/test-submodule

### Steps

_No response_

### Possible Solution(s)

_No response_

### Notes

Looking at the changelogs, there have been some [changes](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/pull/16246) related to git submodules in 1.94. I don't know if it's relevant, but could be related.

### Version

```text

commit-hash: 85eff7c80277b57f78b11e28d14154ab12fcf643

ssl: OpenSSL 3.5.4 30 Sep 2025
os: Mac OS 15.7.4 [64-bit]
```

Suggest indexing for `str::char_indices().skip_while(|(i, _)| *i < index)`

<!--
Hi there! Whether you've come to make a suggestion for a new lint, an improvement to an existing lint or to report a bug or a false positive in Clippy, you've come to the right place.

For bug reports and false positives, please include the output of `cargo clippy -V` in the report.

Thank you for using Clippy!

Write your comment below this line: -->

```rust
let string = "example:hello";
let index = 5;

let result = string
    .char_indices()
    .skip_while(|(i, _)| *i < index)
    .find_map(|(i, c)| if c == ':' { Some(i) } else { None });

assert_eq!(result, Some(7))
```

could be optimized to

```rust
let string = "example:hello";
let index = 5;

let result = string[index..]
    .char_indices()
    .find_map(|(i, c)| if c == ':' { Some(i) } else { None })
    .map(|i| i + index);

assert_eq!(result, Some(7))
```

Indexing operations are faster than skipping to a specific index.

Clippy wrongly reports clippy::large_stack_arrays on static struct

### Summary

Hello, I have a problem with clippy::large_stack_arrays lint.

Clippy reports clippy::large_stack_arrays on a `public static mut` struct defined like

```
/// The global `CmpLog` map for the current `LibAFL` run.
#[no_mangle]
pub static mut libafl_cmplog_map: CmpLogMap = CmpLogMap {
    headers: [CmpLogHeader {
        hits: 0,
        shape: 0,
        kind: 0,
    }; CMPLOG_MAP_W],
    vals: CmpLogVals {
        operands: [[CmpLogInstruction(0, 0); CMPLOG_MAP_H]; CMPLOG_MAP_W],
    },
};
```
and here's the short output from clippy
```
error: allocating a local array larger than 512000 bytes
   --> libafl_targets/src/cmplog.rs:165:19
    |
165 |         operands: [[CmpLogInstruction(0, 0); CMPLOG_MAP_H]; CMPLOG_MAP_W],
```
clippy suggests to put this on heap, but it is not possible because it's a static struct.

Thank you!

### Lint Name

clippy::large_stack_arrays

### Reproducer

1. Clone this repository: `git clone https://github.com/AFLplusplus/LibAFL.git`
2. Checkout to: `git checkout b86314282907aa77d727e3bb9a1b03b75ad441c0`
3. Run clippy: `cargo +nightly clippy --all --all-features`

Clippy reports
```
error: allocating a local array larger than 512000 bytes
   --> libafl_targets/src/cmplog.rs:165:19
    |
165 |         operands: [[CmpLogInstruction(0, 0); CMPLOG_MAP_H]; CMPLOG_MAP_W],
    |                   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
    |
note: the lint level is defined here
   --> libafl_targets/src/lib.rs:7:9
    |
7   | #![deny(clippy::pedantic)]
    |         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
    = note: `#[deny(clippy::large_stack_arrays)]` implied by `#[deny(clippy::pedantic)]`
    = help: consider allocating on the heap with `vec![[CmpLogInstruction(0, 0); CMPLOG_MAP_H]; CMPLOG_MAP_W].into_boxed_slice()`
    = help: for further information visit https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-clippy/master/index.html#large_stack_arrays
```

But, in our code, this is a `pub static mut`struct (https://github.com/AFLplusplus/LibAFL/blob/main/libafl_targets/src/cmplog.rs#L158)
```
/// The global `CmpLog` map for the current `LibAFL` run.
#[no_mangle]

    headers: [CmpLogHeader {
        hits: 0,
        shape: 0,
        kind: 0,
    }; CMPLOG_MAP_W],
    vals: CmpLogVals {
        operands: [[CmpLogInstruction(0, 0); CMPLOG_MAP_H]; CMPLOG_MAP_W],
    },
};
```

and it is not possible to allocate this on heap



### Version


raw_text:
proc-macro derive panics if lifetime is written before the trait

I could trigger the following error message:

```text
error: proc-macro derive panicked
 --> src/bin/serde-test.rs:7:10
  |
7 | #[derive(Serialize)]
  |          ^^^^^^^^^
  |
  = help: message: called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value: "failed to parse derive input: \"struct Test<\\\'a, F> where F: Fn() -> Box< \\\'a + Iterator<Item = usize>> {\\n    __data: PhantomData<F>,\\n}\""

error: Could not compile `genetic_resolver_finding`.
```

This code panics:
```rust
#[derive(Serialize)]
struct Test<'a, F>
where
    F: Fn() -> Box<'a + Iterator<Item = usize>>,
{
    __data: PhantomData<F>,
}
```

while this one doesn't
```rust
#[derive(Serialize)]
struct Test<'a, F>
where
    F: Fn() -> Box<Iterator<Item = usize> + 'a>,
{
    __data: PhantomData<F>,
}
```

Notice how in the first case the lifetime is written before the trait but in the second case it is not.

I use serde_derive in version 1.0.21.
rustc 1.23.0-nightly (45594d5de 2017-11-22)
cargo 0.24.0-nightly (abd137ad1 2017-11-12)

However, both variants compile without problem, if the derive is commented out.

raw_text:
Better derive for trait bounds of generics

Hi,

Thanks a lot for this wonderful crate!!!

I have the following type which I want to serialize:

```rust
#[derive(Serialize)]
struct Response<'a, I>
where
    I: Iterator<Item = &'a Point>,
{
    points: IteratorAdapter<I>,
}
```

I use this wrapper for iterators, but it is not important. The important point is that there is a `Serialize` implementation for the `IteratorAdapter<I>` and of course also for `Point`. The problem is that the derive macro generates the following trait bounds:

```rust
#[automatically_derived]
impl <'a, I> _serde::Serialize for Response<'a, I> where
I: Iterator<Item = &'a Point>, I: _serde::Serialize {
    // some code
}
```

It requires `I: _serde::Serialize`, and it does not compile.
However, the thing which is really needed to be serializable is `IteratorAdapter<I>`. So the correct trait bound should be 
`IteratorAdapter<I>: _serde::Serialize`.

There is a workaround for this by declaring just

```rust
#[derive(Serialize)]
struct Response<Ps>
{
    points: Ps,
}
```

The link to the playground https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2018&gist=f6a9ac1985b570c9357f59bdc052411c

Serialize/deserialize tagged newtype variant containing unit

To me, it seems that a tagged newtype variant containing `()` should be serializable/deserializable in the same way as unit variants. Specificly I have the following enum:

```rust
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize, Debug)]
#[serde(tag = "result", rename_all = "snake_case")]
enum Response<T> {
    Success(T),
    Error {
        ...
    },
}
```

I'd expect `Success(())` to pe deserialized from and serialized to `{ "result": "success"}`, but that doesn't seem to be the case. It doesn't work to deserialize it and when I try to serialize it (with serde_json) I get the following error:

```
Error("cannot serialize tagged newtype variant Response::Success containing unit", line: 0, column: 0)
```

Is there any reason why this doesn't work, or should we fix this? I'd would be happy to make a PR.

Replacement API for Deserializer in-band Signalling

There are quite a few features currently in serde implementations where in-band signalling is used to communicate data from the deserializer into deserialize.  This is turning into quite a big problem over time because it destroys the interoperability of serde in various ways.

A good example is the `arbitrary_precision` flag in `serde_json`. Since serde has no notion of a large integer the deserializer will deserialize numbers internally by emitting an object with a special `$serde_json::private::Number` key which is understood by `serde_json` itself. This however means that if someone tries to use this with other value types (like many libraries have) it will fail.

We use two value types in our own code: we have a fork of serde's internal `Content` type as well as a variation of serde_json's `Value` type that carries additional annotations. Currently if we turn on `arbitrary_precision` as feature we break everything because now any number is emitted as `$serde_json::private::Number` which none of our deserializers support. However we also feel very uncomfortable turning on this feature because even if we fix our own stuff is not now has a chance to break more.

I understand that a correct fix for this is tricky but I do wonder if it makes sense to start extending the underlying serde type system to carry some extension data around because I think this is going to eventually bite us much harder. I'm not entirely what the best solution is but I think extending the list of serde types to carry some internal extension value is most likely going to play a role in it. Similarly to how u128 was retrofitted we could add a new `Signal` value that formats can add extra information to.

Still not sure how to best make interoperability work best. Most likely deserializers should be encouraged to invoke some sort of default behavior when they find something like that.

`broadcast::Receiver` skips some messages when the original receiver isn't used

It seems that when the original receiver created by `broadcast::channel(n);` isn't used (expected dropped) some messages are not picked up by cloned versions of the receiver. 

It is difficult to provide a minimally working example as my use-case was fairly complex, but essentially:
1. Spawn a broadcast channel. 
2. Pass the (clonable) sender to multiple tasks. Those tasks call `.subscribe().recv()` to listen.
3. Send events to the broadcasters. From location A the events were sent, but from location B the events were not sent. Both locations occur on the same sender instance, but one was more deeply nested than the other. 

I'm not entirely sure if this my misuse of the broadcaster or a bug, but all I changed was consuming the original receiver (rather than letting it drop out of function scope) and it started receiving the missing events.

Debugging tokio async application

_Discussion about this future started here #6939._

Hi! I'm interested in improving the debugging process for asynchronous applications. Also i'm a developer of the OS debugger for rust named [bugstalker](https://github.com/godzie44/BugStalker) (bs). Recently bs have some new (and working, but currently in develop branch) functions for async debugging. See this [issue](https://github.com/godzie44/BugStalker/issues/27) with implementation notes, and [this](https://github.com/godzie44/BugStalker/tree/develop?tab=readme-ov-file#async-rust) or [this](https://github.com/godzie44/BugStalker/blob/develop/doc/demo_async_bt.gif) for example of working.

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

The problem is that to get information about workers, tasks, etc., the debugger relies on the details of tokio internal implementation (the names of structure fields, the names of global variables, some types, etc.). It is clear that these details can change from version to version of tokio. Therefore, the implementation in the debugger is currently locked to tokio version 1.41. If you are interested, I see two ways to solve this problem: the least invasive but complicating the implementation on the debugger side, and the more inconvenient for tokio, but more robust from the debugger's point of view.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

_1. Add tokio version into ELF .note section_

I think this a simple way for tokio, but it assumes that the debugger complements the implementation with each new version of tokio runtime (if internal structures is changed). But I think this may be a good point of start.

This information may be added only for debug builds. POC of implementation may be found [here](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/discussions/6939#discussioncomment-11105477). 

_2. Add some specific, debugging information in tokio_ 

This is a harder way. Tokio can add some global data with information needed for debugger. This data can be managed by tokio in debug mode and annotated with `#[cfg(feature = "debug")]`. What debugger needs is described in this [issue](https://github.com/godzie44/BugStalker/issues/27). Also this debug data should have a stable types (from debugger point of view). 

For example

```
#[cfg(feature = "debug")]
static OWNED_TASKS_DEBUG: LinkedList<RawTask> = ...

```

And tokio should manage this list in debug builds.

**Additional context**

I think that such a solution will be very useful for any debugger that will support asynchronous rust, not only bs.

Cannot build docs with --cfg docsrs --generate-link-to-definition

`RUSTDOCFLAGS="--cfg docsrs -Zunstable-options --generate-link-to-definition" cargo doc` does not work on tokio. This also affects downstream users of tokio when `--no-deps` is not passed.

I think this is mainly due to `cfg(windows)` code being enabled, and the definitions for windows-only crates are not found when building on a non-windows platform.

https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/blob/dd74c7c1bfd69ee997c57aade1db2326b85855df/tokio/src/macros/cfg.rs#L37-L47

Introduce `dl` key to allow per-crate download links

This change allows the registry to override its own global `dl` key defined in the root config.json for each package version.

```
    // This optional field specifies the download link for this package
    // only, overriding the global `dl` link declared in the registry's
    // `config.toml`. The `{crate}` markers et al. are not interpolated
    // in this context.
    "dl": "https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/foo/0.1.0/download"
```

### What does this PR try to resolve?

Some third-party 'generic' registries can't (or aren't willing to) support the global 'one `dl` for everything' API that Cargo currently exposes for registries. This change allows much more flexibility by allowing the registry to return unique `dl` links for each individual package version.

### How should we test and review this PR?

Create a new registry with a mock `dl` in the `config.json` and set the real link in the package version JSON line instead.

Add lint for 'toilet closures'

Closes #2523

This name is a little silly, but is also a widely used term and I don't think there is a funnier name we could use.

I feel like the discussion in that issue thread has come to a settle, with most people preferring `drop` to `|_| ()` or suggesting those do not to implement their own `fn ignore<T>(_: T) {}` which would not fire this lint. It is also always possible to disagree with the agreed style of clippy with a simply `allow` attribute.

changelog: [`toilet_closures`]: Implemented lint for replacing `|_| ()` with `drop`

io: drop the `Sized` requirements from `AsyncReadExt.read_buf`

## Motivation

`AsyncReadExt.read_buf` takes both `Self` and its buffer argument by mut ref, yet requires `Sized` for both of them,
disallowing `dyn Trait` for no good reason.

## Solution

Remove the explicit `Sized` requirement for `Self`, and introduce `?Sized` in relevant places.

See also #6161

Hi @nmattia, I went through a similar issue, what I've learned (and consider this just an incomplete/incorrect answer until someone from the Cargo team can add more information) is that `--package` isn't an arbitrary package selection option (that Cargo could eventually resolve from the `Cargo.toml` file) but rather a "whitelist filter" applied to the dependency graph of the workspace being worked on (the current directory if `--manifest-path` isn't specified), analogous to the `--exclude` option that could be seen as the blacklist filter for the same workspace.

In general I think Cargo only sees what's in `Cargo.toml` (independent of the directory structure) and will resort to `Cargo.lock` only for dependency resolution (of packages already discovered through `Cargo.toml`).

(cc'ing @Eh2406 as this might be an opportunity for some minor documentation improvement)

raw_text:
> I don't understand, wouldn't it be easy for application author to not specify an MSRV at all? In this situation, do they run into any problems?

Exactly this. If I do specify `rust-version` in my `Cargo.toml`, this basically _is_ the commitment of following that MSRV and I would prefer that it is be considered if it exists. When I write an application, I usually do not have that property in my `Cargo.toml` and there is nothing there for Cargo to consider in the first place. Hence, I think the presence or absence of the `rust-version` key in the current crate's manifest is a pretty good indicator of intent in both situations.

raw_text:
Some precedents in Cargo

[`cache.auto-clean-frequency`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/config.html#cacheauto-clean-frequency)
- "never" — Never deletes old files.
- "always" — Checks to delete old files every time Cargo runs.
- An integer followed by “seconds”, “minutes”, “hours”, “days”, “weeks”, or “months”

[`resolver.incompatible-rust-versions`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/config.html#resolverincompatible-rust-versions)
- Controls behavior in relation to your [`package.rust-version`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/rust-version.html) and those set by potential dependendencies
- Values:
  - allow: treat rust-version-incompatible versions like any other version
  - fallback: only consider rust-version-incompatible versions if no other version matched

[`package.resolver`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/resolver.html#resolver-versions) is only a version number.  When adding `incompatible-rust-version`, we intentionally deferred anything being done in manifests.

[`[registry]`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/config.html#registry)
- Set default registry
- Sets credential providers for all registries
- Sets crates.io values

[`[registries]`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/config.html#registries)
- Sets registry specific values

`yanked`: can't do new resolves to it but left in if already there. Unstable support to force it with `--precise` but that doesn't apply recursively.

pre-release: requires opt-in through version requirement. Unstable support to force it with `--precise` but that doesn't apply recursively.

We use the term `publish` and not `release`

raw_text:
> If you are wrapping Cargo, what benefit is there for cargo to override these than you too?

Not _that_ much, `cargo-sandbox` can (and does currently) set this, but I thought you'd be interested in it nonetheless as I might not be the only one with this problem.

I guess I'm also arguing from a more philosophical side: the temporary directory is an input to build scripts and to the compiler, and I think Cargo should manage it like it does with all the other inputs.

> What went into the design of `CARGO_TARGET_TMPDIR`? e.g. was this considered and rejected?

I could only find https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/issues/2841 and https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/pull/9375, both of which don't seem to consider this alternative?

> * build-dir vs target-dir

Definitely `build-dir`.

> * old build-dir layout vs new

I'm ambivalent of where exactly this should point, but maybe:
- Build scripts: `build-dir/$PROFILE/build/$PACKAGE-$HASH/tmp`.
- Compiler:
  - Old layout: `build-dir/tmp` (cannot be `build-dir/$PROFILE/tmp` because it conflicts with targets named `tmp`, see https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/pull/9814)
  - New layout: `build-dir/$PROFILE/build/$PACKAGE-$HASH/tmp`.

> * shared caches, requiring the new build-dir layout's unit dir to be a cacheable unit

Hmm, you wouldn't want to cache the temporary directory?

> `cc` uses `OUT_DIR` for this but do we want to have that in the cacheable unit?

EDIT: I'm not familiar with how Cargo intends to cache files, but let's consider e.g. `sccache`. I guess you could choose either way, but I'd probably lean towards "don't cache", most usage of temporary directories that I've seen don't first check if the temporary file exists already, they do "create new dir based on process ID or other random identifier", and then only use it as a scratch space.

> * granular locking

Unsure what you mean here? Anything that uses a temporary directory will figure out locking on its own, this is outside Cargo's control.

Fair, but I still don't really think this is a duplicate or in any way related to the linked issue. They're both about how the lint interacts with unsafe code, but these two issues are about very different operations that are flagged (union access vs unsafe method calls).


Checking if the lazy evaluation is in an unsafe block leads to unnecessary false negatives (e.g. if you're in an `unsafe fn` you're in an unsafe context so we would presumably have to avoid running this lint in there even if there's no unsafe operation performed in the closure at all and where it would be perfectly valid to emit a warning).

I am also interested in this feature. I would like this to choose a common default variant when no `tag` field is available, to only require users to specify a type when using a non-common variant.

I would want the following:
```toml
[[binds]]
address = "0.0.0.0:80"

[[binds]]
type = "tls"
address = "0.0.0.0:443"
cert = "/some/file/path"
```

```rust
#[derive(Deserialize)]
#[serde(tag = "type", rename_all = "snake_case")]
pub enum Bind {
    #[serde(other)]
    Http {
        address: SocketAddr,
    },
    
    #[serde(alias = "tls")]
    HttpsTls {
        address: SocketAddr,
        cert: PathBuf,
    }
}
```
but with `#[serde(other)]` it doesn't currently compile with the error message: `#[serde(other)] must be on a unit variant`

Is there any progress on this issue?

@Diggsey , I use a similar solution based on `untagged` in my project, but it has an important downside that it obfuscates deserialization errors: if the input data is in the wrong format, e.g., it has a known tag but one of the fields associated with this tag is missing, you end up with unhelpful "data did not match any variant" error.

I therefore support @WaffleLapkin 's feature request: it would be great if `serde(other)` allowed non-unit variants.

I think if we add all bells&whistles to syntax highlihting, we'd have to re-implement all of these logic:

https://github.com/rust-analyzer/rust-analyzer/blob/366ad6f03ba2296f09cb79ea139fa53a132fa651/crates/ra_ide_api/src/goto_definition.rs#L56-L131

>besides not doing the NavigationTarget stuff 

That and the lack of index would indeed be the only differences. But **not** using `NavigationTarget` is a key. The philosophical problem with `NavTarget` is that it is an public API type, which is consumed more or less directly by the LSP. So it has API which is good for LSP, but which is a bad fit for rust-analyzer.

To demonstrate the concrete problem, suppose we do use `reference_definition` verbatim in highlighting. And let's say we want to highlight calls to unsafe functions specially. Than, we'd need to figure out if a function is unsafe from it's `NavigationTarget`, and that's  hard because `NavigationTarget` API is not really Rust-specific. It talks about text editor concepts like ranges. 

This "using public API types to build an internal implementation" problem is pretty bad long term. We already suffer from this in `hover`, which currently relies on `reference_definition`, but should be using `classify_reference` as well.

raw_text:
Thanks for the tips!

I implemented granular error reporting for `compile_error!`-based errors and updated existing UI tests as requested.

There were 5 `remote` tests that didn't get updated, from which `missing_field` and `unknown_field` were good already, whereas `wrong_de`, `wrong_ser` and `wrong_getter` deal with generated code that uses the remote type/values, so spans from the user type don't help. I plan to resolve this as well, preferably in this PR, though if there is a need to land this ASAP, I can organize a separate one.

Also a funny error message from `remote/wrong_de` has been reported: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/56335.

Now addessing your points:

> Regarding compile-fail tests, please rebase on master to pick up https://github.com/serde-rs/serde/commit/4821d09a4820d2579da0358ef4be3f8db7d1272d.

> I believe [this line](https://github.com/serde-rs/serde/blob/7d217d7c2ad108591d3613c5da3b21b417eb8919/serde_derive/src/lib.rs#L96) will need to return more information than just a String. You could use [`syn::Error`](https://docs.rs/syn/0.15.22/syn/struct.Error.html) which is basically a String + Span, then use [`to_compile_error()`](https://docs.rs/syn/0.15.22/syn/struct.Error.html#method.to_compile_error) to turn it into a compile_error! with the right span.

Done.

> Some of those changes seem suspicious to me, such as:

That's because previously errors pointed to the whole container while lacking multi-token span support unless `--cfg procmacro2_semver_exempt` is used. Now spans are more precise and rely on the [`syn::Error::new_spanned`](https://docs.rs/syn/0.15.22/syn/struct.Error.html#method.new_spanned) constructor which supports multi-token spans even on stable.

> Ideally the error would point to the `borrow = "'b"` attribute

raw_text:
> I think I would prefer not to make this change (nor the suggested alternative).

What is your reservation with the alternative? It seems like a low/no-maintenance solution (which I'd be happy to implement) that resolves this concern nicely. If the derive doesn't already do this, the only thing that would need to change is that serde should keep the last instance of a given container attribute. 

> Surely the user importing the macro from `serde::Serialize` not `rocket::serde::Serialize` should be fine right?

The idea is that `serde` becomes something that Rocket's users can benefit from right out of the box with no configuration at all. Since the release of 0.5-rc, we've already had a few requests from users hoping to remove `serde` from their dependencies and either 1) being unable to do so, or 2) lamenting the additional `#[serde(crate = "rocket::serde")]`. Most seem to be opting for the latter, so it seems that my desire to not have `serde` be an explicit dependency is shared by Rocket's users as well.

> If not, I would recommend maintaining a rocket-specific fork of serde_derive_internals containing what you need.

This is a much higher maintenance burden that the alternative I proposed above while simultaneously being really suboptimal. It duplicates code and increases compilation time if anyone _does_ depend on `serde` with the `derive` feature enabled.

> As soon as there is a way for macro-generated code to refer reliable to a particular crate in a way that survives re-exports, I would happily adopt that.

As much as I'd like to see this as well, I cannot imagine such a feature being shipped in stable, or at all, any time soon. I'd love to give Rocket's users seamless access to `serde`. This is the only missing puzzle piece.

raw_text:
Remove redundant RepartitionExec from plan

**Is your feature request related to a problem or challenge? Please describe what you are trying to do.**
I was running benchmarks this morning and noticed this fragment of the query plan when running TPC-H query 5.

```
CoalesceBatchesExec: target_batch_size=4096
  RepartitionExec: partitioning=Hash([Column { name: "n_nationkey" }], 24)
    RepartitionExec: partitioning=RoundRobinBatch(24)
      ParquetExec: batch_size=8192,
```

It seems redundant to repartition with round-robin and then immediately repartition again using a hash.

A more complex example:

```
RepartitionExec: partitioning=Hash([Column { name: "r_regionkey" }], 24)
  CoalesceBatchesExec: target_batch_size=4096
    FilterExec: r_name = ASIA
      RepartitionExec: partitioning=RoundRobinBatch(24)
        ParquetExec: batch_size=8192,
```

In this example, we could push the repartition on r_regionkey down to the scan.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Implement new optimizer rule to remove redundant repartitions and/or push down repartitions.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
None

**Additional context**
None

raw_text:
maximum line length

I'd like `ripgrep` to have the ability to either hide or trim lines that are very long. Some lines take up my entire screen and are borderline useless to look at. It's possible that finding an intelligent way to shorten them would be best, since my guess is that the actual matched text is much smaller than the full line. However, this is harder to implement.

I don't think this should be enabled by default. It seems a little surprising for `ripgrep` to hide lines like that. In general, I like the work flow of, "run a search, see huge lines, confirm that I don't care about them and run ripgrep again with an option to hide them." It may however be plausible to enable this limit if results are being dumped to a terminal (we already enable colors, line numbers and file headings).

raw_text:
add support for other text encodings

Right now, ripgrep only supports reading UTF-8 encoded text (even if some of it is invalid). In my estimation, this is probably good enough for the vast majority of use cases.

However, it may be useful to search other encodings. I don't think I'd be willing to, say, modify the regex engine itself to support other encodings, but if it were easy to do transcoding on the fly, then I think it wouldn't add too much complexity. The [`encoding_rs`](https://github.com/hsivonen/encoding_rs) project in particular appears to support this type of text decoding.

Some thoughts/concerns:
- Transcoding would require using the incremental searcher as opposed to the memory map searcher. (Which is fine.)
- Transcoding requires picking a source encoding, and doing this seems non-trivial. You might imagine the CLI growing a new flag that specifies a text encoding, but what happens if you want to search directories containing files with many different types of text encodings? Do we need a more elaborate system? I'm inclined towards not, since I think the juice probably isn't worth the squeeze.

Unhelpful error on Arg parse

For context, this is what was being read in `from_yaml()`:

``` yaml
- es:
  short: e
  help: Sets the ES tag on the output files.
  default_value: 001
  takes_value: true
```

When running my program I got the very confusing:
`thread 'main' panicked at 'called `Option::unwrap()` on a `None` value', ../src/libcore/option.rs:325`

Looking at the backtrace, I was able to narrow it down to a `Arg::from_yaml()` not parsing correctly. But no idea where or why!

The fix was easy: simply wrap 001 in quotes to make it a string. However, it was a bit annoying to figure it out. 

It would be nice to see the context of the `panic!()` in these cases. For example, what arg setting failed.

MsQueue::pop pins epoch until return

The `MsQueue::pop` currently [starts with](https://github.com/aturon/crossbeam/blob/bf1fb5627d67582a53ef712e8cb07fb9ebf878fa/src/sync/ms_queue.rs#L242) a call to `epoch::pin`. This I believe will prevent collection until the method returns, which could potentially take quite a long time (due to the blocking behavior). 

I *think* it may be possible to just drop the epoch [in the blocking case](https://github.com/aturon/crossbeam/blob/bf1fb5627d67582a53ef712e8cb07fb9ebf878fa/src/sync/ms_queue.rs#L298-L301), but that may be naive, so I'd want to think through this some more.

raw_text:
Multiple versions for dependency `autocfg`

#### Summary
Latest release of crossbeam-utils (0.7.0) depends on an old version of autocfg, which triggers the following Clippy warning when used together with other packages and slows down compilation:
```
warning: multiple versions for dependency `autocfg`: 1.0.0, 0.1.7
  |
  = note: `-W clippy::multiple-crate-versions` implied by `-W clippy::cargo`
  = help: for further information visit https://rust-lang.github.io/rust-clippy/master/index.html#multiple_crate_versions
```
The version from git already depends on `autocfg 1`, so it seems it could be fixed by just releasing a new version of crossbeam-utils - the last one is 3 months old.

#### Steps to reproduce
Add these dependencies to your project:
dirs 2.0.2, which depends on dirs-sys -> redox_users -> rust-argon2 -> **crossbeam-utils -> autocfg 0.1.7**
rust-ini 0.15.1, which depends on ordered-multimap -> **hashbrown -> autocfg 1**

Run: `cargo clippy`

raw_text:
crossbeam-epoch's atomic.rs doesn't handle alloc::alloc returning null pointers

In Fuchsia, we're doing an [update](https://fuchsia-review.googlesource.com/c/fuchsia/+/517844) of our vendored version of crossbeam. As part of it, we found some uses of `alloc::alloc` that may be incorrect, like https://github.com/crossbeam-rs/crossbeam/blob/master/crossbeam-epoch/src/atomic.rs#L254. According to the [documentation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/alloc/trait.GlobalAlloc.html#errors) for GlobalAlloc, it's possible for allocation to return a null pointer in two cases:

* memory is exhausted
* layout doesn't match the allocator's size or alignment constraints.

This risks undefined behavior if these conditions are met.

expected tuple struct or tuple variant, found function `Ok`

I was  building [intel-mkl-tool](https://github.com/rust-math/intel-mkl-src) and I found that switching from 1.0.48 to 1.0.49 (and 50 and 51) breaks compilation, which violates semver.

# Steps to reproduce
1. `git clone git@github.com:rust-math/intel-mkl-src.git`
2. `cd intel-mkl-src/intel-mkl-tool`
3. `cargo build --release` produces errors like this (trimmed for brevity):

```
error[E0532]: expected tuple struct or tuple variant, found function `Ok`
  --> intel-mkl-tool/src/entry.rs:75:16
   |
75 |         if let Ok(dir) = std::env::var("OUT_DIR") {
   |                ^^ not a tuple struct or tuple variant
   |
help: consider importing one of these items instead
   |
1  | use core::result::Result::Ok;
   |
1  | use std::result::Result::Ok;
   |

error[E0308]: mismatched types
  --> intel-mkl-tool/src/download.rs:34:17
   |
34 |                 Ok(new_data.len())
   |                 ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ expected enum `WriteError`, found struct `anyhow::Error`
   |
   = note: expected enum `std::result::Result<_, WriteError>`
              found enum `std::result::Result<_, anyhow::Error>`

error[E0308]: `match` arms have incompatible types
  --> intel-mkl-tool/src/config.rs:15:41
   |
15 | #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Display)]
   |                                         ^^^^^^^
   |                                         |
   |                                         expected struct `std::fmt::Error`, found struct `anyhow::Error`
   |                                         `match` arms have incompatible types
16 | pub enum LinkType {
17 |     #[display(fmt = "static")]
   |       ------- this is found to be of type `std::result::Result<(), std::fmt::Error>`
18 |     Static,
19 |     #[display(fmt = "dynamic")]
   |       ------- this is found to be of type `std::result::Result<(), std::fmt::Error>`
   |
   = note: expected enum `std::result::Result<_, std::fmt::Error>`
              found enum `std::result::Result<_, anyhow::Error>`
   = note: this error originates in the derive macro `Display` (in Nightly builds, run with -Z macro-backtrace for more info)
```

Then change `intel-mkl-tool/Cargo.toml` so that it has `anyhow="1.0.48"` and it builds cleanly.

Note that intel-mkl-tool appears unmaintained.

1. `git clone git@github.com:rust-math/intel-mkl-src.git`
2. `cd intel-mkl-src/intel-mkl-tool`
3. `cargo build --release` produces errors like this (trimmed for brevity):

```
error[E0532]: expected tuple struct or tuple variant, found function `Ok`
  --> intel-mkl-tool/src/entry.rs:75:16
   |
75 |         if let Ok(dir) = std::env::var("OUT_DIR") {
   |                ^^ not a tuple struct or tuple variant
   |
help: consider importing one of these items instead
   |
1  | use core::result::Result::Ok;
   |
1  | use std::result::Result::Ok;
   |

error[E0308]: mismatched types
  --> intel-mkl-tool/src/download.rs:34:17
   |
34 |                 Ok(new_data.len())
   |                 ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ expected enum `WriteError`, found struct `anyhow::Error`
   |
   = note: expected enum `std::result::Result<_, WriteError>`
              found enum `std::result::Result<_, anyhow::Error>`

error[E0308]: `match` arms have incompatible types
  --> intel-mkl-tool/src/config.rs:15:41
   |
15 | #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Display)]
   |                                         ^^^^^^^
   |                                         |
   |                                         expected struct `std::fmt::Error`, found struct `anyhow::Error`
   |                                         `match` arms have incompatible types
16 | pub enum LinkType {
17 |     #[display(fmt = "static")]
   |       ------- this is found to be of type `std::result::Result<(), std::fmt::Error>`

19 |     #[display(fmt = "dynamic")]
   |       ------- this is found to be of type `std::result::Result<(), std::fmt::Error>`

```

Then change `intel-mkl-tool/Cargo.toml` so that it has `anyhow="1.0.48"` and it builds cleanly.

raw_text:
Cannot opt out of backtrace feature on nigthly.

Anyhow seems to have include two backtrace strategies: one for stable and one for nightly. The former is managed by default-off Cargo feature "backtrace", but the latter is turned on automatically on nightly regardless of Cargo feature.

This may add more code to the executable, making `anyhow` significantly more bloated compared to `Box<dyn Error+Send+Sync>` in some scenarios. I see 92 additional kilobytes in `.text` section according to `cargo bloat`, which disappear when I manually edit out all Anyhow's code sections with `#[cfg(backtrace)]`.

I think both backtracing modes should be adjustable by Cargo features. Anyhow may check `#[cfg(backtrace)]` only once, e.g. to `compile_error!` if Cargo feature for nightly-style backtraces is enabled on non-nightly. At the very least a negative Cargo feature like `prohibit_backtraces` should be provided to support minified builds. If user builds with `-Zbuild-std-features=panic_immediate_abort` to save kilobytes then backtraces are likely not welcome as well, even if natively supported by the compiler.

Related: #230.

Should there be an `impl std::error::Error for anyhow::Error`?

When `anyhow::Error` is an associated type of a trait, such as `TryFrom`, then calling code cannot propagate the inner `anyhow::Error` into an outer `anyhow::Error` generically, as [this playground](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2021&gist=d86a7e7da19ef81ef3c35a2b6224d844) demonstrates.

In my project I initially thought I could just make the bound precise to `anyhow::Error`, like this:

```
fn do_stuff<T>(arg: T) -> anyhow::Result<()>
  where Thingy: TryFrom<T, Error=anyhow::Error>,
```

-but this precludes other impls that I _do_ want to cover generically, including `impl TryFrom<Thingy> for Thingy` which has `Error = Infallible`. (I'm not sure if this is from a blanket impl in `std` or a dependency I'm using to define `Thingy`.)

-so I attempt to specify all of the `anyhow::Error` construction constraints: 


```
fn do_stuff<T>(arg: T) -> anyhow::Result<()>
  where
    Thingy: TryFrom<T>,
    <Thingy as TryFrom<T>>::Error: 'static + Send + Sync + std::error::Error,
```

Now I can pass any `T` with any `TryFrom` error that can be converted to an `anyhow::Error`. Great!

…except `anyhow::Error` does _not_ implement `std::error::Error`, so it cannot wrap itself.

Is this simply a bug, or is there a design rational for not providing `impl std::error::Error for anyhow::Error` ?

raw_text:
A way to disable anyhow stacktraces (without disabling stacktraces from other crates)

Since https://github.com/dtolnay/anyhow/pull/333 anyhow errors are now capturing a stacktrace at time of creation and including that stacktrace in cases like `format!("{error:?}")`.
We use anyhow for user facing errors, and make use of anyhow's error chaining to provide a nicely formatted sequence of events that led to the error. The stacktrace adds a huge amount of noise to errors that we would like to avoid.
Additionally we need our error cases to be fast and want to avoid capturing a stacktrace for that reason.

This new functionality can be disabled by `RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=0` which is possibly enough in some cases.
However we also manually reimplement our panic handler to give a custom backtrace, and this would be disabled by `RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=0`

raw_text:
#[from] without implicit #[source]

### TL;DR
It would be great to have an equivalent of `#[from]` attribute, which doesn't provide implicitly the functionality of `#[source]`. 
### The setting
I've got an enum:
```rust
#[derive(Error)]
enum MyError {
    Failure(String),
}
```
and a function I didn't write:
```rust
fn fallible() -> Result<(), String> { ... }
```
which I want to use inside my function:
```rust
fn meta_fallible() -> Result<(), MyError> {
    ...
    fallible()?;
    ...
}
```
### The problem
This won't compile and AFAIK there's no ergonomic way to make `MyError` smart enough to make it work.
Right now `meta_fallible` won't be able to convert error `String` to `MyError`, because it lacks right `from`. Let's try to add it:
```rust
#[derive(Error)]
enum MyError {
    Failure(#[from] String),
}
```
Now it won't compile, because while `From<String> for MyError` would be fine, `String` can't be used as `&dyn std::error::Error`, so it will fail as a thing returned from `source`. The only way to bypass this is manual implementation of `From<String> for MyError`.


```rust
fn meta_fallible() -> Result<(), MyError> {
    ...
    fallible()?;
    ...
}
```

This won't compile and AFAIK there's no ergonomic way to make `MyError` smart enough to make it work.
Right now `meta_fallible` won't be able to convert error `String` to `MyError`, because it lacks right `from`. Let's try to add it:
```rust
#[derive(Error)]
enum MyError {
    Failure(#[from] String),
}
```

Generic source compatible with anyhow (or similar)

Sometimes, it may make sense to compose an error enum of generic sources. This is easily possible by using `std::error::Error + 'static` trait bounds:

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Error)]
pub enum FetchError<
    L: std::error::Error + 'static,
    S: std::error::Error + 'static,
> {
    #[error(transparent)]
    Load(L),

    #[error("Failed to save new value")]
    Save(#[source] S),
}
```

This supports errors which implement `std::error::Error` directly, however, it can't be used when the sources are, say, an `anyhow::Error`:

```rust
FetchError<anyhow::Error, anyhow::Error>> =
    |      ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ the trait `StdError` is not implemented for `anyhow::Error`
```

I have seen that thiserror internally uses `thiserror::private::AsDynError<'a>`, but that's (a) a private API and (b) I wouldn't know what to supply as a lifetime parameter when using this as a trait bound.

Could you help me find a way to support both implementations of `StdError` as well as `anyhow::Error` (or other types that dereference to a `dyn StdError`) as generic arguments?
Would it be possible for `thiserror` to simplify these trait bounds in some way?

raw_text:
`anyhow::Error` as `#[source]` does not work generically

With

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Error)]
#[error("uh oh")]
struct FooError<Inner> {
    #[source]
    source: Inner,
}
```

`FooError<anyhow::Error>` does not implement `Error` due to the `Inner: Error` bounds on generic arguments. Meanwhile, as called out in the docs, this _does_ work:

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Error)]
#[error("all good")]
struct FooError {
    #[source]
    source: anyhow::Error,
}
```

since `source` will implicitly deref to `dyn Error`.

Can the docs mention the difference?

Alternatively, is there any way for this to work? It would be nice to generically include a source error that could either be an `Error` itself or dereference to one. Maybe it's relevant that `anyhow::Error` has an `AsRef<dyn Error + Sync + Send + 'static>` impl (though of course you'd know that)

Extract Display derive into separate reusable crate

I stumbled upon #65 while searching for a way to derive Display using this crate without deriving Error at all. The Display impl and `#[error(...)]` syntax is just so good and convenient, I want to use it all over the place. I've seen dispaydoc but I'm not keen on using doc strings for this.

To borrow your ascii diagram from #65...

```
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------->
derive(Error)    derive(Error)  OR  derive(Display)    derive(Error, Display)
#[error(...)]    #[error(...)]      #[display(...)]    #[error(...)] + #[display(...)]

     ^ what most people use        ^ what I am wishing for:                  ^
                                     * use the Display impl from thiserror   |
                                     * no impl of Error                      |
                                                                            /
                                                     where we actually are: 
                                                      * thiserror Error impl
                                                      * 3rd Party Display impl
```

I think it would go something like this:
* break the Display derive out into its own crate
* make thiserror depend on that new crate.
* add `#[display(...)]` to power the Display derive instead of `#[error(...)]` if `#[derive(Error)]` is not present
* reexport the Derive macro from the new crate in thiserror. (this I expect is the most iffy?)

Then everyone can pick and choose whether to derive Error or just derive Display and those implementations are always compatible. Plus there's a nice new but familiar Display derive crate anyone can use.

I'll try and make a branch that simply cuts out the Error derive as a little experiment. See how I get on.

[Feature request] Enabling support for transitive "#[from]' handling

I will explain myself with a very simple example : 

Say I have this huge error type on my codebase : 

```rust
#[derive(Error, Debug)]
pub enum MyError {
    #[error("Network error: {0}")]
    Network(String),

    #[error("Conversion Error: {0}")]
    ConversionError(#[from] ConversionDbError),

    // Around 30 other variants
```

And with 
```rust

#[derive(Error, Debug)]
pub enum ConversionDbError {
    #[error("UUID conversion error: {0}")]
    Uuid(#[from] uuid::Error),

    #[error("UTF-8 conversion error: {0}")]
    FromUtf8(#[from] std::string::FromUtf8Error),

    #[error("TryFromIntError conversion error: {0}")]
    TryFromInt(#[from] std::num::TryFromIntError),
}
```

I still need to add the manual conversions in order to forward the error down my enum : 
```rust
impl From<uuid::Error> for DbError {
    fn from(e: uuid::Error) -> Self {
        Self::ConversionError(ConversionDbError::Uuid(e))
    }
}
// and the 2 others
```

This kindof takes away my goal from importing the `thiserror` crate, which is to reduce boilerplate redundant code to the maximum. Of course, the code above isn't my production code. My code is so huge that this kind of feature will make it way more human-friendly.

Am I doing smth wrong or this is a feature that can be implemented ?

Any suggestion solve the problem will be appreciated.
Thank you.

raw_text:
Always use consistent triangle winding

**Describe the bug**
As described in https://docs.rs/epaint/0.8.0/epaint/struct.Triangles.html#structfield.indices , `egui` isn't consistent in which order it generates vertices for triangles, so you have to disable backface culling.  Personally I consider this poorly behaved, and it makes life more complicated for a user or renderer for no particular gain.  This makes it more troublesome to integrate egui with various graphics systems or game libs.  

In `tetra` for example you have to switch the winding mode whenever you draw `egui` stuff, then switch it back unless you're fine drawing the backs of every triangle.  Some frameworks, like `ggez`, don't even have an option to switch winding mode, so you can't use `egui` with them.  Enabling backface culling also improves performance slightly, and having to switch it back and forth to draw GUI stuff certainly degrades it.

**To Reproduce**
N/A, documented behavior.

**Expected behavior**
Only ever generate triangles with a CCW winding.  A simple but perhaps slow method would be to just walk through all the triangles before they're drawn and re-order their indices appropriately; I can try to submit a PR to do this if you want.  I don't know enough about `egui`'s internals to know more.

**Desktop (please complete the following information):**
 - OS: n/a
 - Browser: n/a
 - Version: 0.8.0

raw_text:
Possible to delete a buffer that is mapped asynchronously

The library doesn't correctly detect if a buffer is mapped for the matter of cleaning it up. We are only checking for the pending map operation on the GPU: https://github.com/gfx-rs/wgpu/blob/4fdb54d33a38632ee111465e4c8282dc95994aa8/wgpu-core/src/device.rs#L302

Instead, we need to turn this into an enum:
```rust
enum MapState {
  Waiting, // waiting for GPU to be done before mapping
  Active, // mapped
  Idle, // not mapped
}
```

Rename Leptos config options to kebab-case via serde, instead of replacing characters

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

My app is using a bigger config file, which contains a member of the `leptos::LeptosOptions` type. The config is serialized as a `.toml`, which adheres to the `kebab-case` naming convention. Since `leptos::LeptosOptions` does not use `#[serde(rename_all = "kebab-case")]`, if I want to deserialize it, I would need to specify all Leptos options I set under the snake_case.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Add `#[serde(rename_all = "kebab-case")]` to the `leptos::LeptosOptions` struct. This can be easily done by modifying the [this line](https://github.com/leptos-rs/leptos/blob/main/leptos_config/src/lib.rs#L25).

```rust
// ...
#[derive(TypedBuilder, Debug, Clone, serde::Deserialize)]
#[serde(rename_all = "kebab-case")]
pub struct LeptosOptions {
// ...
```

This would also lead to not needing to [replace '-' characters in the *entire* config file](https://github.com/leptos-rs/leptos/blob/main/leptos_config/src/lib.rs#L180).

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

Duplicating the Leptos config options in a struct I own, using the rename method and implementing `From<T>` to allow conversion to `leptos::LeptosOptions`. This seems however a bit meaningless, since Leptos *already* uses kebab-case, just not in a manner in which it could satisfy my use case. 

**Additional context**

Example of my `config.toml`:

```toml
log-level = "Debug"
application-address = "0.0.0.0:3000"

# ...

[leptos]
output-name = "my-awesome-app"
# ...
```

My `config.rs`:

```rust
#[derive(Deserialize)]
#[serde(rename_all = "kebab-case")]
pub(crate) struct Config {
    #[serde(default = "default_application_address")]
    pub application_address: String,

    #[serde(
        default = "default_log_level",
        deserialize_with = "deserialize_log_level"
    )]
    pub log_level: Level,

    pub leptos: LeptosOptions,
}
```

Point search too slow

Hi, Thank you for this amazing project.
I am planning to get help in creating a vector search engine with qdrant.
I created a collection like below using docker container.

```python
url = f"{qdrant_host}/collections/{model_name}"
        data = {
            "name": model_name,
            "distance": "Cosine",
            "vector_size": 768
        }
        response = requests.put(url,
                                headers={'Content-Type':'application/json; charset=utf8'},
                                data=json.dumps(data))
```

I put points like below.

```python
batch = []
for payload, embedding in data:
  """
  payload = {
                  'short_str1': str,
                  'integer_format_date_1': integer,
                  'list_of_str1': list,
                  'integer_format_date_2': integer,
                  'short_str2': str,
                  'list_of_str2': list
              }
  """
  batch.append({
                                'id': cnt,
                                'payload': payload,
                                'vector': embedding
                            })
  cnt += 1

qd_url = f"{qdrant_host}/collections/{model_name}/points"
response = requests.put(qd_url,
                                        headers={'Content-Type':'application/json; charset=utf8'},
                                        data=json.dumps(data))
```

Loaded about 620,000 points. It takes about 10-20 seconds to search for a point as shown below.

```python
data = {
        'vector': embedding,
        'with_payload': True,
        'score_threshold': 0.8,
        'top': 10
    }
qd_url = f"{qdrant_host}/collections/{model_name}/points/search"
response = requests.post(qd_url,
                             headers={'Content-Type':'application/json; charset=utf8'},
```

Must finish() be called after sending data?

After sending data by SendStream, I must call finish() to make peer receive data. 
```
send.write_all(request.as_bytes())
    .await
    .map_err(|e| anyhow!("failed to send request: {}", e))?;
send.finish()
    .await
    .map_err(|e| anyhow!("failed to shutdown stream: {}", e))?;
```

But I want to use the same stream to send data and peer can receive data every time. I don't know how to make it, because SendStream has no  method flush(). 
Client:
```
send.write_all(b"hello")
    .await
    .map_err(|e| anyhow!("failed to send request: {}", e))?;
send.flush()

send.write_all(b"world")
    .await
    .map_err(|e| anyhow!("failed to send request: {}", e))?;
send.flush()

send.finish()
    .await
    .map_err(|e| anyhow!("failed to shutdown stream: {}", e))?;
```

Server:
```
let resp = recv
        .read_to_end(usize::max_value())
        .await
        .map_err(|e| anyhow!("failed to read response: {}", e))?;
```

```
        .read_to_end(usize::max_value())
        .await
        .map_err(|e| anyhow!("failed to read response: {}", e))?;
println!("recv: {:?}", resp1);
```

raw_text:
Split crates between user and implementor APIs

As discussed in #188, it would be useful to have a clearer separation between interfaces that are stable for users to invoke versus those that are needed for *implementing* parallel traits. We would like to reach Rayon 1.0 fairly soon, but it would be a shame to have to lock down "internal" details too. If we can split that into a separate crate, then it can have its own versioning, with more frequent semver bumps that don't impact "plain" Rayon use. This should also fix #177, as we can document all the gory details that we currently hide from regular users. 

CC @bluss who was pressing for better policy around API boundaries.  And I'm signing myself because I'm interested and I think I have a good feel for how to do this. 😀

raw_text:
Communication costs are quadratic in the number of worker threads

As a side effect of profiling Stylo for
https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1371496, I picked up some
numbers for Rayon too.

I ran the Stylo benchmark in the abovementioned bug with 1, 4, 16 and 64
worker threads, on Valgrind/Callgrind configured for fine-grain thread
interleaving -- basically all threads move forwards together.

Looking at the costs (in instructions executed, and inclusive of callees)
for rayon_core::registry::WorkerThread::wait_until, I see a cost increase
which looks extreme as the number of threads increases (MI = million insns):

p1      137.1 MI
p4      238.4 MI  (1.7 x p1)
p16    3568.7 MI  (15.0 x p4)
p64  177089.5 MI  (49.6 x p16)

In the worst case (p64), wait_until and callees use 177 G insns, of which
about 129 G are in calls to <coco::deque::Stealer<T>>::steal.

Looking at the code for rayon_core::registry::WorkerThread::steal, it appears that
each thread inspects the work queues of all other threads.  So Rayon induces
communication costs in the underlying machine that are at least quadratic in
the number of threads.

Given that this is measured on a simulator that slows down progress hugely,
I wouldn't pay too much attention to the exact numbers.  But it is clear
that Rayon might have scaling problems, especially in cases like this where
(I think) there is actually very little work to do, and so the threads spend
a lot of time searching for work.  (But then why don't they end up going to
sleep?  Maybe they do.  I don't know.)

SpiDevice's interface can't be used for streaming transactions

There are applications where, when writing data to an SPI device, it is more efficient to write the data in a single transaction rather than multiple transactions (my use case is an SPI screen that can write multiple lines in a single transaction).

However, with the current `SpiDevice` interface, I would need to create a slice of `Operation`s in order to be able to write all the lines in a single transaction. Because I need a new Operation for each separate line, this requires 128 lines * 8 bytes per slice = 1KiB of additional data just for the pointers (the framebuffer itself is only 2 KiB!). The chip I am targeting only has 40KiB of memory total, so this is a substantial amount of overhead.

The interface is now stabilized because the crate is at 1.0, but is there some change that can be made to improve this situation? (e.g. an interface that takes an iterator of `Operations`, a closure-based interface, or something similar)

Proposal: add a pre-commit config for `rustfmt --check` + file hygiene?

Would you accept a small PR adding `.pre-commit-config.yaml` to this repo?

```yaml
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/pre-commit/pre-commit-hooks
    rev: v4.6.0
    hooks:
      - id: trailing-whitespace
      - id: end-of-file-fixer
      - id: check-yaml
      - id: check-merge-conflict
      - id: check-added-large-files
  - repo: local
    hooks:
      - id: rustfmt
        entry: cargo fmt -- --check
        language: system
        types: [rust]
        pass_filenames: false
```

The intent is to catch formatting drift at commit time so it doesn't reach reviewers. Clippy intentionally not included — it recompiles per run; better as CI.

Happy to skip if not wanted, or to adjust the hook set if you'd prefer different defaults.

raw_text:
If a request to the playground errors, no indication is ever shown as such in the UI

Right now, if you view TRPL locally via `rustup doc --book`, the playground requests [will all fail because of the playground's current CORS settings](https://github.com/integer32llc/rust-playground/issues/194). 

But even if those worked, if you didn't currently have internet acccess and tried to click the play button from the local copy of the book, the playground requests would also fail.

In these situations currently, the markup just shows "Running..." forever because [there's only a `success` handler for the request](https://github.com/azerupi/mdBook/blob/35a447d08aaf6ef7308ebf461ea9cb9645e729d4/src/theme/book.js#L323-L335). It would be nicer if an error message was displayed if something went wrong with the request.

raw_text:
serve: double reload on backup files deletion

The problem arises when working with an editor like [Kate](https://kate-editor.org/) which keeps your current edits in a swap file.

When saving the swapped contents to the real file an event occurs and triggers the rebuild of the book.
While the book is building another event occurs because the swap file is deleted. 

On my machine this creates a race. 
Sometimes the second thread is fast enough to delete the folder before the first finishes working and nothing happens.
But around 50% of the time the deletion happens right after the first build finished. This means the browser will receive a reload command at the same time as the second thread starts deleting the files. In that case the browser gets a 404 and the reload function is dead. A manual reload is required now.

I see a probable solution by triggering the rebuild with some delay on the server.
Delaying the client is also possible but the client would either have to poll the server for the file or delay a fixed amount of time.
What do you think?

raw_text:
Provide "infallible" numeric-parsing for captures

This is a feature request that is mostly just for ergonomics, but could hypothetically permit some good optimizations as well.

When matching against text that includes string-representations of numeric data, the regex patterns used in matching *should* guarantee that the capture groups are valid stringified numbers. For instance, given this pattern:

    \w+ : (\d{1,5})$

...a valid match will always have exactly one capture, and that capture will correspond to an integer with at most five decimal digits. This is guaranteed to be a valid positive numeric value within the range of 32-bit and larger integer types.

But, given a valid `Captures` generated from this regex called `c`, the simplest way to parse the integer as `u32` (and `panic` on failure, since this should be an infallible operation) seems to be:

        c.get(1).unwrap().as_str().parse::<u32>().unwrap()

It would be nice if there were some way to guarantee (either at Regex-compile time, or, ideally, at Rust-compile time) that, for a given pattern, a particular capture group (1) will exist if there is a match (avoiding the first `unwrap`), and (2) that it can be parsed as a numeric type (avoiding the second `unwrap`). Given these guarantees, it would be nice to have an ergonomic way to actually do that parsing.

Guaranteeing the capture-group index would of course be easier with const-generics, so that may be out of the question for now. But providing a limited version of this feature that would help with many or most typical cases might not be too bad, e.g.:

* Create a new `ValueRegex<T>` struct representing a compiled regex pattern with *exactly one* capture-group representing a numeric type, where `T` is the numeric type
   * A pessimistic validation of the capture-group pattern should be fine, at least for now. For instance, there could be some simple rules permitting a small number of "permissible" patterns for a given `T`.
   * The most flexible/robust solution would probably be to use T::FromString somehow, but I think that would require modifying the actual regex syntax. For instance, it could be something like:

          r"foo: (?V<u32>)$"
     ... where `?V<T>` is used to indicate that the capture-group content corresponds to a string representation of type `T`. The `ValueRegex<T>` type would internally contain something like a compiled version of the pattern `foo: (.+?)$`, and matching would be a two-step process wherein, following a successful regex match, `T::FromStr` would be used to attempt to parse the group `(.+?)`; if the parse is successful, the value is saved internally, and if not, the entire match fails.
* `ValueRegex<T>` could implement mostly the same interface as `Regex`, but in addition it would have:
       fn find_value(&self, text: &'t str) -> Option<T>      // This will *only* fail if `text` does not contain the pattern!

Using it would look something like:

    let RE = ValueRegex::<u32>::new(r"\w+ : (\d{1,5})$").unwrap();
    some_function(RE.find_value("foo: 243\n")?);

Provide "infallible" numeric-parsing for captures

This is a feature request that is mostly just for ergonomics, but could hypothetically permit some good optimizations as well.

When matching against text that includes string-representations of numeric data, the regex patterns used in matching *should* guarantee that the capture groups are valid stringified numbers. For instance, given this pattern:

    \w+ : (\d{1,5})$

...a valid match will always have exactly one capture, and that capture will correspond to an integer with at most five decimal digits. This is guaranteed to be a valid positive numeric value within the range of 32-bit and larger integer types.

But, given a valid `Captures` generated from this regex called `c`, the simplest way to parse the integer as `u32` (and `panic` on failure, since this should be an infallible operation) seems to be:

        c.get(1).unwrap().as_str().parse::<u32>().unwrap()

It would be nice if there were some way to guarantee (either at Regex-compile time, or, ideally, at Rust-compile time) that, for a given pattern, a particular capture group (1) will exist if there is a match (avoiding the first `unwrap`), and (2) that it can be parsed as a numeric type (avoiding the second `unwrap`). Given these guarantees, it would be nice to have an ergonomic way to actually do that parsing.

Guaranteeing the capture-group index would of course be easier with const-generics, so that may be out of the question for now. But providing a limited version of this feature that would help with many or most typical cases might not be too bad, e.g.:

* Create a new `ValueRegex<T>` struct representing a compiled regex pattern with *exactly one* capture-group representing a numeric type, where `T` is the numeric type
   * A pessimistic validation of the capture-group pattern should be fine, at least for now. For instance, there could be some simple rules permitting a small number of "permissible" patterns for a given `T`.
   * The most flexible/robust solution would probably be to use T::FromString somehow, but I think that would require modifying the actual regex syntax. For instance, it could be something like:

          r"foo: (?V<u32>)$"
     ... where `?V<T>` is used to indicate that the capture-group content corresponds to a string representation of type `T`. The `ValueRegex<T>` type would internally contain something like a compiled version of the pattern `foo: (.+?)$`, and matching would be a two-step process wherein, following a successful regex match, `T::FromStr` would be used to attempt to parse the group `(.+?)`; if the parse is successful, the value is saved internally, and if not, the entire match fails.

       fn find_value(&self, text: &'t str) -> Option<T>      // This will *only* fail if `text` does not contain the pattern!

Method to get maximum number of bytes necessary for match

TL;DR: Is there a way to ask a `Regex` struct the number of bytes it needs to see to find a match? Basically I’m interested in streaming matches. 

I’m a little fuzzy on exactly what I’m thinking of for this, so I’ll start with my intended use case to avoid an XY problem. 

I’m experimenting with extending the `im` crate to provide an immutable string based on their `Vector` type. I’m thinking through the various uses of std’s `String` and trying to port them to my new type. I started wondering how to do searches on this new kind of string, which is essentially a discontiguous rope, and realized it’s kind of nontrivial to do a regex search because matches might be found on the boundary between two contiguous chunks of the full string. 

So I thought it could be interesting to provide an interface to allocate a buffer of some kind that can store at least the necessary number of bytes for a regex match. 

For example, for the regex `(hi|hello)`, I figure you never need to look at more than five bytes at a time to determine if there’s a match. So I can just search contiguous strings like normal, then load the last five bytes of the str and the first five of the next into the buffer, search that like normal, and then continue into the next contiguous str like normal. 

I haven’t worked out all the details yet, but the general strategy relies on being able to ask the `Regex` type how many bytes I need to see at a time. Do you know if there’s a way to do that, or if not, how hard such an API addition would be?

why is rustlings lsp not on by default?

I was doing exercises using VSCode and rust-analyzer, and was confused and frustrated for nearly 30 minutes about why rust-analyzer was not working for my exercises. I thought my VScode and rust-analyzer were broken, and went down many false paths, especially since there are already many other cases of rustlings-analyzer being completely broken (which was *not* the case here!)

Only after more than 30 min of googling did I realize that I needed to opt IN to this by doing `rustlings lsp`. What a horrible user-unfriendly experience! How are new users supposed to know that they need to do this command in order to get this to work?

Any way to just remove the step of requiring to `rust-analyzer lsp`, so that it simply works out of the box? This extra step is very, very easy to miss for rustlings' target audience, and really left a bad impression when I ran into it.

edit: if it's not practical to remove the requirement to do `rust-analyzer lsp`, one alternative I would be okay with is to more loudly advertise this fact; this would save a lot of confusion and frustration for rustlings target audience.

raw_text:
OSX binaries don't run on older machines

Like with https://github.com/Diggsey/multirust-rs/issues/23, building for OSX can be nontrivial sometimes to ensure that something works on older machines. I _think_ that OSX doesn't need the same "CentOS 5 craziness" that Linux needs, but rather it can just set the `MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET` environment variable to "10.7". To the best of my knowledge, that will instruct the linker to "do the old things" which I think is the only point of incompatibility.

"Thankfully" the OpenSSL OSX has and depends on is basically locked at 0.9.8, so no need to worry about that in this case!

raw_text:
Linux binaries don't run on older machines

Unfortunately to get a "maximally compatible" linux binary it needs to be built on a super-old Linux machine (e.g. CentOS 5). This is what we currently do for our rustc distribution, but otherwise the error message you get looks like:

```
./multirust: /rustroot/lib64/libcrypto.so.1.0.0: no version information available (required by ./multirust)
./multirust: /lib64/libc.so.6: version `GLIBC_2.14' not found (required by ./multirust)
./multirust: /rustroot/lib64/libssl.so.1.0.0: no version information available (required by ./multirust)
```

This should be "easily" available through a docker image of CentOS 5 on Travis. You can see [our docker image](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-buildbot/blob/master/slaves/dist/Dockerfile), although that level of complexity probably isn't necessary (e.g. the custom gcc may not be needed).

Another point is that to distribute a linux binary with SSL support the only robust way I know of is to link OpenSSL statically. Older systems don't have the 1.x releases of OpenSSL and still use 0.9.8, so to work on both you've got to statically link in OpenSSL (e.g. this is what Cargo does).

I can certainly help out with all this stuff as well!

Portability

It should be noted in some obvious place that this library is not portable (and therefore should not be used if the user aims for their application to be portable), due to its dependency on `ring`, which only provides support for `x86(_64)`, `aarch64` and some variants of 32-bit ARM due to requiring arch specific assembly implementations from BoringSSL without providing portable fallbacks for them.
